Pre-indexed code knowledge graph, auto syncs on code changes, for Claude Code, Codex, Gemini, Cursor, OpenCode, AntiGravity, Kiro, CoPilot, and Hermes Agent — fewer tokens, fewer tool calls, 100% local

https://colbymchenry.github.io/codegraph/

CodeGraph

Already installed? Run codegraph upgrade

Follow @getcodegraph on X for updates.

Supercharge Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, OpenCode, Hermes Agent, Gemini, Antigravity, Kiro, GitHub Copilot, and more with Semantic Code Intelligence

The fastest complete code graph · surgical context · built for how agents actually work · 100% local

  **Kernel powered by Rust**

Documentation & Website →


The CodeGraph platform is coming — for every PR, know exactly what to test, what could break, which flows are affected, and whether business logic is compromised.

Get early beta access to the hosted product · getcodegraph.com

Contents

  • Get Started
  • Language Support
  • Why CodeGraph?
  • Key Features
  • Framework-aware Routes
  • Mixed iOS / React Native / Expo bridging
  • Quick Start
  • How It Works
  • CLI Reference
  • MCP Tools
  • Library Usage
  • Configuration
  • Telemetry
  • Verified releases
  • Supported Platforms
  • Supported Agents

  • Troubleshooting

Get Started

1. Install the CLI

No Node.js required — one command grabs the right build for your OS:

# macOS / Linux
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/colbymchenry/codegraph/main/install.sh | sh

# Windows (PowerShell)
irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/colbymchenry/codegraph/main/install.ps1 | iex
Already have Node? Use npm instead (works on any version) 
npm i -g @colbymchenry/codegraph

CodeGraph bundles its own runtime — nothing to compile, no native build, works the same everywhere. The installer puts codegraph on your PATH but doesn't change your current shell — open a new terminal before the next step so the command resolves.

Upgrade any time with codegraph upgrade — it detects how you installed (bundle, npm, or npx) and updates in place. Add --check to see if an update is available, or codegraph upgrade <version> to pin one. After an upgrade, codegraph status and your agent tell you when a project's index was built by an older version: run codegraph index there to rebuild it.

2. Wire up your agent(s)

In a new terminal, run the installer to connect CodeGraph to the agents you use:

codegraph install

Detects and auto-configures Claude Code, Cursor, Codex CLI, opencode, Hermes Agent, Gemini CLI, Antigravity IDE, Kiro, GitHub Copilot (VS Code, Copilot CLI, JetBrains IDEs), IBM Bob, Factory Droid, Windsurf, Qwen Code, DeepSeek Harness, Grok Build, Kimi Code, Qoder CLI, and Pi — wiring the CodeGraph MCP server into each. This is the step that connects CodeGraph to your agent; installing the CLI in step 1 does not do it on its own. It only wires up your agent — it does not index any code; building each project's graph is the separate codegraph init in step 3. (Shortcut: npx @colbymchenry/codegraph downloads and runs this in one go.)

3. Initialize each project

cd your-project
codegraph init

codegraph init creates the local .codegraph/ directory and builds the full graph in the same step — one command, done.

4. No more syncing!

Auto-sync is enabled by default. CodeGraph watches the project and updates the graph on every file change — while your agent edits code, or you add, modify, or delete files. The index is never stale, and there is nothing to re-run.

Uninstall

Changed your mind? One command removes CodeGraph from every agent it configured and the CLI itself — every install it finds (standalone bundle, npm global package, launcher link), shown to you before anything is deleted:

codegraph uninstall

Pass --keep-cli to remove only the agent configurations and keep the CLI installed.

Reverses the installer — strips CodeGraph's MCP server config, instructions, and permissions from each configured agent. Your project indexes (.codegraph/) are left untouched; remove those per-project with codegraph uninit. Use --target to remove from specific agents, or --yes to run non-interactively.

Language Support

Every language below gets the same treatment — full structural extraction and cross-file resolution into one graph, no per-language setup:

Per-language details — extensions, frameworks, and what exactly gets extracted — in Supported Languages.

Why CodeGraph?

When an AI agent needs to understand code — to answer a question or make a change — it discovers structure the slow way: grep, glob, and Read, one file at a time, rebuilding call paths and dependencies by hand. That's a pile of tool calls and round-trips before it even starts the real work.

CodeGraph hands the agent the exact code it needs in one call. It's a pre-built knowledge graph of every symbol, call edge, and dependency in your codebase — so instead of crawling files, the agent asks one question and gets back the relevant source, the call paths between those symbols (including dynamic-dispatch hops grep can't follow), and the blast radius of a change. Surgical context, not a file-by-file search — which means fewer tool calls and faster answers on every codebase, large or small.

A note on cost: CodeGraph's win on every codebase is precision — the agent stops crawling files and answers from the graph. On current models that precision is also a large direct saving: the 2026-08 re-measurement, on a harness that blocks the CLI in both arms, put it at 44% lower cost and 62% fewer tokens on average across the seven benchmark repos, because a strong model without the graph burns its budget re-deriving structure. Cost tracks how much discovery a question demands more than raw repo size: 57–78% on questions the file-reading agent needed 28–43 tool calls to answer, near-even where it got there in 7.

A note on context: the numbers above measure throughput — tokens processed, tools called, dollars spent to reach one answer. They don't measure what is still sitting in your context window afterward, and on that axis CodeGraph costs more, not less. Across the same seven repos in multi-turn sessions, CodeGraph's responses leave about 80% more retrieval context resident at the end of a session than a file-reading agent's do — on VS Code, 67k tokens against 18k. The mechanism is the same one that makes it fast: CodeGraph returns one dense, verbatim payload that answers the question and then stays in the window, where a grep-and-read agent churns through many small results that get evicted. Fewer tokens processed and a larger persistent footprint are both real at once. If you run long sessions in a small window, budget for it. Measured per-repo: docs/benchmarks/residual-context-occupancy.md.

Benchmark Results

Tested across 7 real-world open-source codebases spanning 7 languages, comparing an agent (Claude Code, headless) answering one architecture question with and without CodeGraph, at the median of 4 runs per arm. Re-measured 2026-08-05 on Claude Opus 4.8 against the current build, on a harness that blocks the codegraph CLI in both arms — contamination row: 0 of 28 without-arm runs.

The universal win — every repo, every size: 88% fewer tool calls · 53% faster · 62% fewer tokens · 44% cheaper · file reads cut to zero on all seven repos.

With the index available, the agent answers from one to four codegraph_explore calls and stops. Without it, the agent burns its budget on discovery — up to 43 tool calls and 19 file reads re-deriving what the graph already knew. Built for speed — the Rust kernel

CodeGraph's parsing engine is a native Rust kernel: 20 languages — TypeScript, JavaScript, Java, Python, Go, C, C++, Rust, C#, Ruby, PHP, Swift, Kotlin, Scala, Dart, R, Lua, Luau (Metal and CUDA ride the C++ path) — parse in compiled code with one boundary crossing per file. Every language shipped only after its graphs proved byte-for-byte identical to the reference engine on real repositories, from small libraries up to the Linux kernel; platforms without a prebuilt binary and files with syntax errors fall back per-file automatically, same graph either way.

And it scales itself to the machine it's on. Worker pools, parallel resolution, and analysis caches are sized from what the system actually has — real core counts (container/cgroup-aware, so a VPS that grants 2 cores gets sized for 2, not the host's 64), honestly-measured available RAM on macOS and Linux, and the measured cost of your project's resolution work:

  • On a workstation: the full parallel pipeline — native parse workers, a multi-worker resolver pool that engages the moment it pays for itself, memory-gated analysis caches. The Swift compiler repository (27k files of Swift and C++) fresh-indexes in about 100 seconds; a one-file edit re-syncs in ~4.
  • On a 2-core / 6GB VPS: the same graph, from a pipeline tuned to finish — the Linux kernel (70k files, 2M symbols, 6.4M relationships) indexes to completion in under 12 minutes where RAM-first designs run out of memory before reaching 1%.
  • Every day after day one: saving a file updates the graph in well under a second — the watcher fires 300ms after a lone save and syncs exactly what changed (~0.3s of work on a 4,400-file project, ~0.4s on the 27,000-file Swift compiler repo), never re-scanning the tree. Measured against the fastest competing indexer's re-index-on-change: 2–7× faster on medium and larger repos across a 31-repo, 30-language benchmark — and the gap widens with repo size, because their cost grows with the repository and ours grows with the change.

How auto-syncing works — and why you don't need to run codegraph sync manually

When your agent (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, opencode) launches codegraph serve --mcp, three layers keep the index in step with your code — and make sure the agent never gets a silent wrong answer in the brief window between an edit and the next sync:

  1. File watcher with debounced auto-sync. A native FSEvents / inotify / ReadDirectoryChangesW watcher captures every source-file create / modify / delete and triggers a re-index after a debounce window (default 2000ms, tunable via CODEGRAPH_WATCH_DEBOUNCE_MS, clamped to [100ms, 60s]). Bursts of edits collapse into a single sync. On a large TypeScript or Vue repo nearly every edit also asks for a repo-wide rebuild of the synthesized callback and event edges; CODEGRAPH_SYNTH_MIN_INTERVAL_MS (1s to 24h) bounds how often that runs, and a rebuild a sync puts off runs when the interval is up. Until then those edges can be that far behind the code, and tool output doesn't say so.

  2. Per-file staleness banner. During the brief debounce window, MCP tool responses that would reference a still-pending file prepend a ⚠️ banner naming it and telling the agent to Read it directly. Pending files NOT referenced by the response surface as a small footer instead. Either way, the agent gets an explicit signal — validated with Claude Code, where the agent literally says "Reading the file directly for the live content" before opening it.

  3. Connect-time catch-up. When the MCP server (re)connects, codegraph runs a fast (size, mtime) + content-hash reconciliation against the working tree before answering the first query — so edits made while no MCP server was running (a git pull from the terminal, edits from another editor, a previous agent session that exited) get absorbed on the next session's first tool call.

agent writes src/Widget.ts
  → watcher fires (<100ms)
  → debounce (default 2s)
  → sync; Widget.ts is in the index
  → next agent query sees it

Verify any time with codegraph status (CLI). If anything is pending, you'll see a ### Pending sync: section naming the files and their edit age.

The handful of cases where manual codegraph sync makes sense: the watcher is disabled (sandboxed environments, or CODEGRAPH_NO_DAEMON=1), or you're scripting against the index outside an agent session and want a pre-flight sync at the start of your script.

Agent Tool Guidance

CodeGraph's MCP server delivers its usage guidance to your agent automatically, in the MCP initialize response. In short, it tells the agent to:

  • Answer structural questions directly with CodeGraph — it is the pre-built index, so a grep/read loop just repeats work it already did. Treat the returned source as already read.
  • Reach for codegraph_explore for almost anything — "how does X work", a flow/"how does X reach Y", or surveying an area. One call returns the relevant symbols' verbatim source grouped by file, the call paths between them (dynamic-dispatch hops included), and a blast-radius summary. Name a file or symbol in the query to read its current line-numbered source.
  • Trust the results — don't re-verify with grep, and check the staleness banner after edits.
  • Works per project: query any project that has a .codegraph/ index by passing projectPath — so a monorepo where only some services are indexed, or a second repo, works in one session. A path with no index returns clean guidance to use built-in tools; indexing stays your decision.

The exact text is src/mcp/server-instructions.ts — the single source of truth for the main agent. Because subagents and non-MCP harnesses never see the MCP guidance, the installer also writes a short marker-fenced section into the agent's instructions file pointing at the codegraph explore CLI equivalent.

fi

MCP Tools

When running as an MCP server, CodeGraph exposes a single tool — codegraph_explore. Measured agent behavior showed that one strong tool steers agents better than a menu of narrower ones — fewer mis-picks, and it saves context every session:

Tool Purpose
codegraph_explore Answer almost any question in one call — "how does X work", a flow ("how does X reach Y"), or surveying an area — returning the relevant symbols' verbatim source grouped by file, plus the call paths between them and a blast-radius summary. Surfaces dynamic-dispatch hops (callbacks, React re-render, interface→impl) grep can't follow. Name a file or symbol in the query to read its current line-numbered source, the same shape the Read tool gives you. A query that names one symbol, like "who calls toValidURL?", gets that symbol's source and every line that uses it, each with the function it sits in and the line's text.

The other tools (codegraph_node, codegraph_search, codegraph_callers, codegraph_callees, codegraph_impact, codegraph_files, codegraph_status) stay fully functional but unlisted by default — everything they return already arrives inline on codegraph_explore (its blast-radius section, the relationship map, a symbol's body as its callee list). Re-enable any of them for the MCP surface with the CODEGRAPH_MCP_TOOLS environment variable (e.g. CODEGRAPH_MCP_TOOLS=explore,node,search,callers), or use their CLI equivalents (codegraph node / query / callers / callees / impact / files / status).

Even when the server's own root has no .codegraph/ index, the tools stay available: pass projectPath to query any indexed project — a sub-service in a monorepo, or a second repo — in the same session. A path that has no index returns clean guidance to use built-in tools instead, so nothing fails loudly, and indexing stays your decision.

Library Usage

CodeGraph can be embedded directly. The npm package re-exports its programmatic API, so both import and require resolve the CodeGraph class in your own process — handy for embedding it in an app (e.g. an Electron main process).

import CodeGraph from '@colbymchenry/codegraph';
// CommonJS works too:
//   const { CodeGraph } = require('@colbymchenry/codegraph');

const cg = await CodeGraph.init('/path/to/project');
// Or: const cg = await CodeGraph.open('/path/to/project');

await cg.indexAll({
  onProgress: (p) => console.log(`${p.phase}: ${p.current}/${p.total}`)
});

const results = cg.searchNodes('UserService');
const callers = cg.getCallers(results[0].node.id);
const context = await cg.buildContext('fix login bug', { maxNodes: 20, includeCode: true, format: 'markdown' });
const impact = cg.getImpactRadius(results[0].node.id, 2);

cg.watch();   // auto-sync on file changes
cg.unwatch(); // stop watching
cg.close();

Lower-level building blocks are exported from the same entry point for callers that drive the graph directly: DatabaseConnection, QueryBuilder, getDatabasePath, initGrammars / loadGrammarsForLanguages, and FileLock.

Embedding requirements

  • Install from npm (npm i @colbymchenry/codegraph) so the matching per-platform package — which carries the compiled library and its dependencies — is fetched alongside the shim.
  • The API runs on your runtime, so it needs Node 22.5+ for the built-in node:sqlite (Electron qualifies when its bundled Node is 22.5+). The CLI and MCP server are unaffected — they run on the self-contained bundled runtime.
  • TypeScript types ship with the package. As with any Node-targeting library, keep @types/node available and skipLibCheck: true (the common default).

Configuration

Next to none — CodeGraph is zero-config by default, with nothing to write or keep in sync to get started. Language support is automatic from the file extension; there's nothing to wire up per language. The one optional file is for mapping custom file extensions.

What it skips out of the box:

  • Dependency, build, and cache directories — node_modules, vendor, dist, build, target, .venv, Pods, .next, and the like across every supported stack — so the graph is your code, not third-party noise. This holds even with no .gitignore. A build folder inside src/ is the exception: no build step writes TypeScript, JSX, Vue, Svelte, Astro, Go, C# or Rust files into one, so those are indexed from it, and a Java, Kotlin or Scala package named build is indexed whole.
  • Anything in your .gitignore — honored in git repos via git, and in non-git projects by reading .gitignore directly (root and nested).
  • Files larger than 4 MB — generated bundles, minified JS, vendored blobs. codegraph status names any source file left out for its size.

To keep something else out, add it to .gitignore. To pull a default-excluded directory back in (say you really do want a vendored dependency indexed), add a negation — !vendor/. The defaults apply uniformly, so committing a dependency or build directory doesn't force it into the graph; the .gitignore negation is the explicit opt-in.

.gitignore can't drop a directory you've committed, though. For a vendored theme or SDK that's checked into the repo (e.g. a Metronic theme under static/), list it under exclude in codegraph.json — gitignore-style patterns, matched against repo-root-relative paths, honored on index, sync, and watch:

{
  "exclude": ["static/", "**/vendor/**"]
}

Conversely, when real source is gitignored on purpose — a project under a second VCS (SVN, Perforce) that .gitignores its own source so it stays out of Git — force it back in with include (the opposite of exclude; includeIgnored only revives embedded git repos, not plain source):

{
  "include": ["Tools/", "Local/typescript/"]
}

CodeGraph discovers those files off disk, overriding .gitignore, on index, sync, and watch. An explicit exclude still wins, and built-in skips (node_modules, dist, .git) are never re-included.

Sometimes a directory shouldn't leave the index — you still want to find things in it — it just shouldn't outrank your real code. A scripts/ or optional-skills/ tree whose helpers use generic names (usage, status, run) can win on an exact name match and crowd out the product code that actually answers the query. Name those trees under deprioritize:

{
  "deprioritize": ["optional-skills/", "scripts/"]
}

This is the ranking counterpart to exclude: those paths stay indexed and findable — searching for them directly still works — they just stop winning against first-party code. It applies to query / search and to explore's ranking. It is not a filter: unlike the built-in example/, sample/, fixture/, benchmark/ and demo/ handling — which also drops those files from some result sets outright — deprioritize only ever changes rank. Reach for exclude when you want something gone.

Custom file extensions

If your project uses a non-standard extension for a supported language — say .dota_lua for Lua, or .tpl for PHP — those files are skipped by default, because the extension isn't one CodeGraph recognizes. Map them with an optional codegraph.json at your project root:

{
  "extensions": {
    ".dota_lua": "lua",
    ".tpl": "php"
  }
}

Each value is a supported language id. The mappings merge on top of the built-in defaults and win on conflict, so you can also re-point a built-in (e.g. ".h": "cpp"). Commit the file to share the mapping with your team. A typo'd language or a malformed file is warned about and skipped — it never breaks indexing — and a project with no codegraph.json behaves exactly as before. Re-index (codegraph index) after adding or changing mappings.

PHP includes from the web root

PHP code often loads files from the folder the web server serves, as in require $_SERVER['DOCUMENT_ROOT'] . '/inc/header.php'. That folder is set in the server's configuration, not in your code, so CodeGraph works it out from your includes: it's the folder under which their paths name files your project has. When they don't settle it (fewer than three different paths, or two folders that fit them about as well), name it in codegraph.json:

{
  "webRoot": "public"
}

The folder is relative to the project root, like "public", "web" or "htdocs", or "." for the root itself, and a webRoot you set always wins. Without either, these includes link to nothing rather than to a guess, which could be a different file of the same name. The next sync applies a change. Includes built from the including file's own folder, like __DIR__ . '/inc/a.php', need neither.

Telemetry

CodeGraph collects anonymous usage statistics — which tools and commands get used, which languages get indexed — to guide where language and agent support work goes. Never any code, paths, file or symbol names, queries, or IP addresses; usage is aggregated locally into daily totals before anything is sent, and the ingest endpoint is public code in this repo that enforces the documented field list. The installer asks up front; turn it off any time:

codegraph telemetry off    # or: CODEGRAPH_TELEMETRY=0, or DO_NOT_TRACK=1

To turn it off for one MCP server entry only, such as one in a config you share, add --no-telemetry to its arguments: codegraph serve --mcp --no-telemetry. That covers the background server it starts too.

TELEMETRY.md lists every field, with the off-switches and the full data-handling story.

Verified releases

Every artifact is built and published by the public Release workflow — never from a laptop — and carries cryptographic proof of it:

  • npm packages are published via trusted publishing (OIDC — no long-lived npm tokens exist that could be stolen) with provenance attestations linking every version to the exact commit and workflow run that built it. Verify what's installed:

    npm audit signatures

  • GitHub Release bundles (and SHA256SUMS) carry signed build attestations (SLSA v1.0 Build Level 2). Verify any downloaded bundle:

    gh attestation verify codegraph-darwin-arm64.tar.gz -R colbymchenry/codegraph

  • The bundled Node.js runtime is checked against the SHA-256 checksums nodejs.org publishes before it goes into a bundle.

Releases published before July 2026 predate this pipeline and don't carry attestations.

Supported Platforms

Every release ships a self-contained build (bundled Node runtime — nothing to compile) for all three desktop OSes, on both Intel/AMD (x64) and ARM (arm64):

Platform Architectures Install
Windows x64, arm64 PowerShell installer or npm
macOS x64, arm64 shell installer or npm
Linux x64, arm64 shell installer or npm

See Get Started for the one-line install commands.

Supported Agents

The interactive installer auto-detects and configures each of these — wiring up the MCP server, which delivers its own usage guidance. For Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, opencode, Factory Droid, Qwen Code, DeepSeek Harness, Grok Build, Kimi Code and Pi it also writes a short marker-fenced CodeGraph section into the agent's instructions file (CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md / GEMINI.md / QWEN.md, or rules/codegraph.md for Grok Build), so subagents and non-MCP agents learn the codegraph explore command:

  • Claude Code
  • Cursor
  • Codex CLI — the Codex IDE extension reads the same config: a global install writes $CODEX_HOME/config.toml (default ~/.codex/config.toml), and a local install writes .codex/config.toml, which Codex uses only in a project you've marked as trusted
  • opencode — MCP entry is OpenCode 2's mcp.servers.codegraph with codemode: false (keeps codegraph_explore on the native tool list; codegraph install migrates the older mcp.codegraph shape)
  • Hermes Agent

  • Kiro
  • GitHub Copilot — Copilot Chat in VS Code (copilot-vscode), the Copilot CLI (copilot-cli), and the Copilot plugin in JetBrains IDEs (copilot-jetbrains)
  • IBM Bob (bob) — Bob IDE and Bob Shell: ~/.bob/settings/mcp.json, or .bob/mcp.json in a project
  • Factory Droid (droid) — ~/.factory/mcp.json, or .factory/mcp.json, which is meant to be committed; Droid reloads the file on its own
  • Windsurf (windsurf) — global only: ~/.codeium/windsurf/mcp_config.json, which Devin, Windsurf's new name, imports by default
  • Qwen Code (qwen) — settings.json in $QWEN_HOME (default ~/.qwen) or .qwen/, keeping any comments in it
  • DeepSeek Harness (dsh) — global only: one entry in $DSH_HOME/cordis.patch.yml (default ~/.dsh) covers every profile

Troubleshooting

"CodeGraph not initialized" — Run codegraph init in your project directory first.

Answers still look like the old version after an upgrade — Re-index each project with codegraph index. Most fixes take effect when a file is indexed, so an index an older version built keeps its old links until then. codegraph status says when a project's index was built by an older version, and your agent's first answer in that project warns you once.

CodeGraph won't use a folder as a project — CodeGraph never treats a system folder such as /, /etc or C:\Windows as a project, nor ~/.ssh, ~/.gnupg, ~/.aws, ~/.config or any folder inside them, whichever link, junction or spelling of the path leads there. The MCP server won't make one a session's default project either, so start your agent in the project's own folder.

Indexing is slow — Check that node_modules and other large directories are excluded. Use --quiet to reduce output overhead.

MCP hits database is locked — current builds shouldn't: CodeGraph bundles its own Node runtime and uses Node's built-in node:sqlite in WAL mode, where concurrent reads never block on a writer. If you still see it:

  • You're on an old (pre-0.9) install. Reinstall to get the bundled runtime — curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/colbymchenry/codegraph/main/install.sh | sh (macOS/Linux), irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/colbymchenry/codegraph/main/install.ps1 | iex (Windows), or npm i -g @colbymchenry/codegraph@latest.
  • codegraph status shows Journal: other than wal — WAL couldn't be enabled on this filesystem (common on network shares and WSL2 /mnt), so reads can block on writes. Move the project (with its .codegraph/ folder) onto a local disk.

MCP server not connecting — Your agent starts the server itself, so you don't launch it by hand. Make sure the project is initialized and indexed (codegraph status) and that the path in your MCP config is correct. If it still won't connect, re-run codegraph install to rewrite the config.

Two codegraph serve --mcp on one project fight over the index / auto-sync stops — CodeGraph allows one live MCP writer per project (the shared background daemon, or a single direct-mode process). Extra clients should proxy to that daemon. If you set CODEGRAPH_NO_DAEMON=1, run only one serve --mcp for that project; a second instance exits with a clear writer-lock error (see writer.pid under .codegraph/). Prefer leaving the daemon enabled so multiple MCP hosts share one watcher.

MCP tool calls fail with Transport closed while codegraph status/sync are healthy — almost always WSL2 with the project on a Windows drive (a /mnt/c or /mnt/d path), where the local socket CodeGraph uses to share one background server across sessions is unreliable. CodeGraph works around this itself now: when the project's filesystem can't host that socket, the shared server puts it in the system temp directory instead, and when the shared server still can't be reached, or drops, the session is served in-process instead of losing the connection. If you still hit it, set CODEGRAPH_NO_DAEMON=1 in your MCP server's environment to skip the shared server entirely (each session runs in its own process). Moving the project onto the Linux-native filesystem (e.g. under ~/ instead of /mnt/) restores the shared server.

Missing symbols — The MCP server auto-syncs on save (wait a couple seconds). Run codegraph sync manually if needed. Check that the file's language is supported and isn't inside a .gitignored or default-excluded directory (e.g. node_modules, dist).

Sharing one checkout between Windows and WSL — Don't point both at the same .codegraph/: the background-server lock and the SQLite index are tied to the OS that wrote them, and SQLite locking across the WSL2/Windows filesystem boundary is unreliable (WSL reports it as a disk I/O error). For a project on a Windows drive (a /mnt/c/… path), WSL keeps its own index automatically: an index first built from WSL goes in .codegraph-wsl/, leaving .codegraph/ to Windows. An index already in .codegraph/ stays where it is, so if Windows built that one, give WSL its own by setting CODEGRAPH_DIR=.codegraph-wsl in WSL and running codegraph init there. CODEGRAPH_DIR always picks the name when set, on either side. CodeGraph skips any sibling .codegraph-* directory when indexing and watching, so the two never trip over each other.

Very large repositories (hundreds of thousands of files), or a large .codegraph/codegraph.db-wal file — The -wal file is SQLite's write-ahead log: writes waiting to be folded into codegraph.db. While a big index is being built, CodeGraph lets it grow in proportion to the index (soft threshold = the larger of 256 MB and a quarter of the index size, up to 2 GB) before folding it back, because folding too often is what made large indexes slow on ordinary disks. At rest it is trimmed to 64 MB, and a leftover from a killed session is folded and trimmed the next time the project opens — the index itself has no size limit. Two environment variables tune this: CODEGRAPH_WAL_VALVE_MB (the soft threshold during indexing) and CODEGRAPH_WAL_HEAL_MB (the resting size and the trim threshold). CODEGRAPH_WAL_VALVE_DEBUG=1 prints every decision to stderr.

Contributing

See CONTRIBUTING.md to build from source, test a change and prepare a pull request. The documentation index links to the project's guides and design notes.

WebGL2 powered visualization framework

https://deck.gl

deck.gl | Website

GPU-powered, highly performant large-scale data visualization

deck.gl is designed to simplify high-performance, WebGL2/WebGPU based visualization of large data sets. Users can quickly get impressive visual results with minimal effort by composing existing layers, or leverage deck.gl's extensible architecture to address custom needs.

deck.gl maps data (usually an array of JSON objects) into a stack of visual layers - e.g. icons, polygons, texts; and look at them with views: e.g. map, first-person, orthographic.

deck.gl handles a number of challenges out of the box:

  • Performant rendering and updating of large data sets
  • Interactive event handling such as picking, highlighting and filtering
  • Cartographic projections and integration with major basemap providers
  • A catalog of proven, well-tested layers

Deck.gl is designed to be highly customizable. All layers come with flexible APIs to allow programmatic control of each aspect of the rendering. All core classes such are easily extendable by the users to address custom use cases.

     All tasks complete!

You: /openspec-archive-change
AI:  Archived to openspec/changes/archive/2025-01-23-add-dark-mode/
     Specs updated. Ready for the next feature.
What do the specs actually look like?

Plain Markdown — requirements with concrete scenarios, no special syntax to learn. Here's what goes in the specs/ folder created above:

## ADDED Requirements

### Requirement: Theme selection
The app SHALL let users switch between light and dark themes,
defaulting to the system preference.

#### Scenario: User toggles dark mode
- **WHEN** the user clicks the theme toggle
- **THEN** the app switches to dark mode and persists the choice

Your AI writes these; you review the plan before any code is written.

OpenSpec is built with OpenSpec — browse this repo's live specs and in-flight changes for real examples at scale.

OpenSpec Dashboard

Why teams adopt OpenSpec

Solo, OpenSpec keeps you and your AI honest on a single repo. On a team, the hard part moves: a feature spans the API server, the web app, and a shared library; requirements are owned by one team and consumed by others; planning starts before any code exists.

Stores are the answer — planning in a repo of its own. The same openspec/ shape you already know (specs and changes), shared by git push like anything else. One source of truth your whole team and every coding agent can read, across every repo.

  • Cross-repo features — one change, one plan, even when the code lands in three repos.
  • Shared requirements — a platform team owns the specs; product teams reference them read-only, right where their coding agent can read them. No drifting wiki.
  • Plan before code — capture the plan in the store now; the code repos catch up later.

Stores are in beta. Start with the Stores guide.

Quick Start

Install OpenSpec. On macOS or Linux, in your terminal:

curl -fsSL https://openspec.dev/cli/install.sh | sh

On Windows, in PowerShell:

irm https://openspec.dev/cli/install.ps1 | iex

Prefer a package manager? npm install -g @fission-ai/openspec@latest (needs Node.js 22.20.0 or higher) or the official Homebrew formula, brew install openspec.

Then navigate to your project directory and initialize:

cd your-project
openspec init

Want your AI to do it? Paste the setup prompt into your coding assistant — it installs the CLI, runs openspec init, and verifies the result.

Now talk to your AI:

  • Not sure what to build yet? Start with /openspec-explore, a no-stakes thinking partner that reads your code, weighs options, and shapes a plan before any code gets written. (Quickstart)
  • Already know what you want? Go straight to /openspec-propose <what-you-want-to-build>.

Both are in the default profile. If you want the expanded workflow (openspec-new-change, openspec-continue-change, openspec-ff-change, openspec-verify-change, openspec-bulk-archive-change, openspec-onboard), select it with openspec config profile and apply with openspec update.

These are skills. Most tools invoke them as /openspec-propose and Codex as $openspec-propose, or you can ask for the work in plain words. openspec init prints the right form for the tools you picked — see Supported Tools. Coming from 1.x and its /opsx:* commands? See Upgrade to 2.0.

Note

Not sure if your tool is supported? View the full list – we support 30+ tools and growing.

Also works with npm, Homebrew, pnpm, yarn, bun, and Nix. See installation options.

Docs

Full documentation lives at openspec.dev/docs.

→ Quickstart: your first change, start to finish
→ Set up your project: what openspec init installs
→ CLI: terminal reference
→ Supported Tools: tool integrations & install paths
→ Customize: profiles, project config, and schemas
→ Stores: plan in a separate repo, shared across your team (beta)
→ Community Showcase: projects and resources built with and for OpenSpec

Community schemas

Third-party schema bundles distributed via standalone repositories — these provide opinionated workflows that integrate OpenSpec with other tools, similar to how github/spec-kit's community extension catalog handles tool integrations.

→ Browse the catalog in the customization docs.

Why OpenSpec?

AI coding assistants are powerful but unpredictable when requirements live only in chat history. OpenSpec adds a lightweight spec layer so you agree on what to build before any code is written.

  • Agree before you build — human and AI align on specs before code gets written
  • Stay organized — each change gets its own folder with proposal, specs, design, and tasks
  • Work fluidly — update any artifact anytime, no rigid phase gates
  • Use your tools — works with 30+ AI assistants via skills

How we compare

vs. Spec Kit (GitHub) — Thorough but heavyweight. Rigid phase gates, lots of Markdown, Python setup. OpenSpec is lighter and lets you iterate freely.

vs. Kiro (AWS) — Powerful but you're locked into their IDE and limited to Claude models. OpenSpec works with the tools you already use.

vs. nothing — AI coding without specs means vague prompts and unpredictable results. OpenSpec brings predictability without the ceremony.

Updating OpenSpec

Upgrade the CLI

With the standalone install, run openspec install. If you installed with npm:

npm install -g @fission-ai/openspec@latest

If you installed OpenSpec with Homebrew:

brew upgrade openspec

Refresh agent instructions

Run this once to refresh the skills installed on your machine. If your team keeps skills in Git, run it in each project that commits them.

openspec update

Usage Notes

Model selection: OpenSpec works best with high-reasoning models. We recommend Codex 5.5 and Opus 4.7 for both planning and implementation.

Context hygiene: OpenSpec benefits from a clean context window. Clear your context before starting implementation and maintain good context hygiene throughout your session.

Contributing

Every change starts as an issue. We discuss it there, and if we agree to pursue it, a maintainer implements the change or invites you to build it with us.

→ CONTRIBUTING.md: the full process, from first issue to merged PR

Other

Telemetry

OpenSpec collects anonymous usage stats.

We collect only command names and version to understand usage patterns. No arguments, paths, content, or PII. Automatically disabled in CI.

Opt-out (any one is enough):

  • openspec config set telemetry.enabled false (global config; unset means on)
  • export OPENSPEC_TELEMETRY=0 or export DO_NOT_TRACK=1 (env overrides config)
Maintainers & Advisors

See MAINTAINERS.md for the list of core maintainers and advisors who help guide the project.

License

MIT

item.title: solidjs/solid
item.description:
A declarative, efficient, and flexible JavaScript library for building user interfaces.

https://solidjs.com

Website • Docs • Tutorial • Playground • Discord

Solid is a declarative JavaScript library for building user interfaces. Instead of a Virtual DOM, it compiles templates to real DOM nodes and updates them with fine-grained reactivity. Declare your state and use it throughout your app — when a piece of state changes, only the code that depends on it re-runs.

At a glance

import { createSignal } from "solid-js";
import { render } from "@solidjs/web";

function Counter() {
  const [count, setCount] = createSignal(0);
  const doubled = () => count() * 2;

  // The component body runs once. Only `{doubled()}` updates when count changes.
  return <button onClick={() => setCount(c => c + 1)}>{doubled()}</button>;
}

render(() => <Counter />, document.getElementById("app")!);

Try it in our Playground.

Explain this!

Solid compiles your JSX to real DOM operations at build time. The component function runs once on mount; reactivity is per-expression, not per-render. The {doubled()} expression compiles to a tracked update that only touches that one DOM position when count() changes.

import { template, delegateEvents, insert } from "@solidjs/web";
import { createSignal } from "solid-js";

const _tmpl$ = /*#__PURE__*/ template(`<button>`);

function Counter() {
  const [count, setCount] = createSignal(0);
  const doubled = () => count() * 2;

  return (() => {
    const _el$ = _tmpl$();
    _el$._$$click = () => setCount(c => c + 1);
    insert(_el$, doubled);
    return _el$;
  })();
}
delegateEvents(["click"]);

Reads update on the next microtask (or call flush() for synchronous interop). Effects are split into a tracking compute phase and a side-effecting apply phase — see the docs for the full model.

Key features

  • Fine-grained updates to the real DOM — no virtual DOM diff.
  • Declarative reactive primitives (createSignal, createMemo, createStore).
  • Render-once components — your component function is plain JavaScript that runs once.
  • Automatic dependency tracking — reading reactive state subscribes to it.
  • Microtask-batched updates with flush() for synchronous interop.
  • First-class async: any computation can return a Promise/AsyncIterable; <Loading> is the boundary.
  • Optimistic UI primitives (createOptimistic, createOptimisticStore) and structured action(...) mutations.
  • Streaming SSR and progressive hydration.
  • TypeScript-first, JSX-first, web-component friendly.
  • Universal: write custom renderers via @solidjs/universal to target non-DOM platforms.

Quick start

Start from a template:

npx degit solidjs/templates/solid-v2/basic my-app
cd my-app
npm install
npm run dev

Or add Solid to an existing Vite project:

npm i solid-js @solidjs/web
npm i -D vite @solidjs/vite-plugin

// vite.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from "vite";
import solid from "@solidjs/vite-plugin";

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [solid()]
});

and point TypeScript at the web JSX types:

{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "jsx": "preserve",
    "jsxImportSource": "@solidjs/web"
  }
}

solid-js owns renderer-neutral component types, while renderer packages such as @solidjs/web and @solidjs/h own their JSX namespaces and jsx-runtime type entries.

Coming from Solid 1.x?

Read the migration guide. Solid 1.x is maintained on the 1.x branch, installs with npm i solid-js@v1-latest, and its docs are at v1.solidjs.com.

For LLMs / AI assistants

The public API differs from any Solid examples that predate 2.0. Before generating Solid 2.0 code, read:

  • packages/solid/skills/solid-2.0/SKILL.md — the primer: the three rules that matter most, the 1.x → 2.0 corrections, and the primitives to reach for, in under 8 KB.
  • packages/solid/CHEATSHEET.md — one-page reference; the bottom enumerates patterns that changed from 1.x.
  • documentation/solid-2.0/MIGRATION.md — full migration guide.
  • docs.solidjs.com — the docs, with /llms.txt and /llms-full.txt.

The primer and the cheatsheet ship inside the solid-js npm package (node_modules/solid-js/skills/solid-2.0/SKILL.md, node_modules/solid-js/CHEATSHEET.md; the build also emits the cheatsheet as the solid-2.0-cheatsheet skill). The packages carry the tanstack-intent keyword, so skill registries that scan node_modules find them.

Repository

This is a PNPM workspaces monorepo. The core runtime (solid-js, @solidjs/signals, @solidjs/web, @solidjs/universal, @solidjs/diagnostics) always shares one version. The two compilers share a version when they release together, and @solidjs/h, @solidjs/html and @solidjs/element version on their own.

Package Path Purpose
solid-js packages/solid Core runtime — components, flow controls, context, hydration.
@solidjs/signals packages/signals Reactive primitives — signals, memos, effects, stores.
@solidjs/web packages/web Web platform runtime — render, hydrate, SSR, Portal, dynamic.
@solidjs/h packages/h Hyperscript / JSX factory.
@solidjs/html packages/html Build-less tagged template literals.
@solidjs/universal packages/universal Universal runtime for custom renderers.
@solidjs/element packages/element Web Components wrapper.
@solidjs/compiler packages/compiler Native Oxc JSX compiler.
@solidjs/babel-plugin packages/babel-plugin Babel plugin for JSX compilation.
@solidjs/diagnostics packages/diagnostics Dev-only diagnostics and attribution harness for tests and agents.

Runtime DOM operations live in @solidjs/web (and @solidjs/universal / @solidjs/h / @solidjs/html). The JSX compilers and the DOM runtime live in this repo, so file their issues here, not on DOM Expressions. The API reference in one page is packages/solid/CHEATSHEET.md, and the design notes are under documentation/solid-2.0/.

Why Solid?

Performant

Engineered for performance with years of research behind it — Solid's runtime cost is close to optimized vanilla JavaScript on the JS Framework Benchmark. Small, fully tree-shakable, fast on the server too. (Read more about Solid's performance.)

Powerful

Performant state management is built in (Context, Stores, Projections). Async is a first-class capability of computations, with <Loading> / <Errored> boundaries and isPending for revalidation indicators. Full SSR, streaming, and progressive hydration when you're ready to move to the server.

Pragmatic

Components are plain functions. Rendering is determined by how state is used — no rendering system to learn. Read-write segregation is encouraged but not enforced.

Productive

Built on JSX and TypeScript, integrates with the Vite ecosystem. Bare-metal abstractions give you direct access to the DOM. Growing ecosystem of primitives, component libraries, and build-time utilities.

More

  • Documentation
  • Tutorial
  • Examples
  • Playground

Browser support

SolidJS Core supports the last 2 years of modern Firefox, Safari, Chrome, and Edge (desktop and mobile). IE and similar sunset browsers are not supported. For server environments, Node LTS, the latest Deno, and Cloudflare Worker runtimes are supported.

Community

Come chat on Discord. Solid's maintainers are active there, and we're always looking for contributions.

Contributors

Open Collective

Support us with a donation and help us continue our activities. [Contribute]

Sponsors

Become a sponsor and get your logo on our README on GitHub with a link to your site. [Become a sponsor]

item.title: NYLLON-SOFTWARE/SignuDoc
item.description:
Open-source document signature platform. Not affiliated with DocuSign.

An e-signature app for your own organization, on your own Vercel account.
Upload a PDF, place fields, send signing links, and keep the sealed, signed copy with its audit certificate.


or copy this to your LLM

Features · SignuDoc vs DocuSign · What it costs · Get started · Self-hosting guide

Why SignuDoc

No seats to pay for. SignuDoc is open source, and the Deploy button sets it up on free plans from Vercel, Neon and Resend, which carry about 250 documents a month for $0. A 15-person team pays DocuSign $8,100 a year for Business Pro seats, or $5,400 for Standard. SignuDoc costs the same whether one person sends or fifty.

No envelope allowance to watch. DocuSign's Standard and Business Pro plans include 100 envelopes per user per year. SignuDoc has no limit of its own. What you can send depends on your hosting plans, and the free ones carry about 250 documents a month.

Your documents stay in your accounts. PDFs live in a private Vercel Blob store and everything else in a Neon Postgres database, both in your name and in the region you choose. Nobody else hosts your agreements, and the code is yours to read, change and run.

Evidence anyone can check. Every finished PDF and its audit certificate carry a PAdES seal that PDF readers check for changes, the audit trail is hash-chained so an edited or deleted row shows, and anyone holding a copy can check it on the install's public Verify page.

One click, nothing to look after. The Deploy button creates the database, the file store and email for you, on free plans. There are no servers to patch, and every push to your copy deploys again.

Everything it takes to get a document signed

Prepare a document in minutes

Upload a PDF, add up to 25 signers in the order they sign, or have some of them sign at the same time, and add people who only receive the finished copy. Then place fields where they belong: signature, initials, date, name, text, number, checkbox, dropdown and radio buttons, each required or optional and each tied to one signer.

The organization, people and documents in these screenshots are made up.

Signing without an account

Each signer gets a link by email, agrees to use electronic records, and signs with a typed or drawn signature on any phone, tablet or computer. Fields from earlier signers stay visible and locked. Signers can download the document before they sign, or decline with a reason, and the sender is told.

Know who is signing

For documents that need more than an email link, ask a signer for an access code you give them yourself, or have SignuDoc email a one-time code when they open the link. The audit certificate records how each signer was checked, with their IP address and browser.

Follow every envelope

The dashboard shows each document as a card with its first page, its status (draft, sent, completed, declined, voided or expired) and who it waits on, with search and a status filter. Each envelope has its own signing deadline, from 3 to 90 days, which you can change while it is out, and automatic reminders every 1, 2, 3 or 7 days, on top of the reminder you can send by hand. If a signer's email address was wrong, correct it after sending: the old link stops working and the new address gets a fresh invitation. A finished envelope can be copied into a new draft with the same document, signers and fields.

Templates for the documents you send every week

Open any envelope and choose Save as template. The template keeps the document, the fields and the signing order, with roles instead of names. Using it asks who signs this time and opens a draft ready to send. Send to many takes a CSV of names and addresses and sends one envelope per row.

Send from your other apps

Your own apps can send documents through SignuDoc's API. An administrator makes a key under Settings, and one call creates an envelope from a PDF with its signers and fields, and sends it. Signed webhooks tell your app when an envelope is sent, viewed, signed, completed, declined, voided or expires. Embedded signing shows the signing page inside your own site, for the sites an administrator allows. The API guide has the details, and /api/v1/openapi.json on your install describes every endpoint.

Sealed, certified, and checkable by anyone

When the last signer finishes, SignuDoc builds the signed PDF and an audit certificate, seals both, and emails them to every signer and copy recipient. Names and text in Latin, Greek, Cyrillic, Chinese, Japanese and Korean scripts are drawn correctly. Anyone can drop a copy on the Verify page to see whether it is exactly the file the site produced; the file never leaves their device, only its fingerprint does.

Your name, logo and color

Signers see your organization, not SignuDoc. Give the install your name, logo and brand color, and they appear on the site, the signing pages and every email. Serve it at your own domain and link your own terms and privacy policy.

Run by your administrators

The first account is the administrator, and you can make more. Choose who may create an account: people at your email domains, nobody, or anyone. People who only sign never need one. Set how long finished documents are kept, and answer a signer who asks for their data with a built-in export or erasure tool.

Administrators see every member's sent and finished envelopes in an "Everyone's" view of the dashboard, and can delete a finished one: it is deleted 14 days later, after the sender has been emailed, and any administrator can cancel in between. Drafts stay private to the person writing them.

Sign-in security, backups and audits

  • Single sign-on over OpenID Connect, with Okta, Microsoft Entra ID, Google Workspace and others, and password sign-in turned off if you want.
  • Two-step sign-in with an authenticator app and backup codes, which administrators can require of everyone who signs in with a password. Single sign-on relies on your identity provider's own check instead.
  • Session limits and lockout: sign people out after a time without use, and stop sign-in for an address after ten wrong passwords.
  • A site audit trail of sign-ins, role changes, deletions and settings, also written to the function logs as JSON so a Vercel log drain can deliver it to your SIEM.
  • Daily backups of the database and files to a second private Blob store, with a script that restores them. See Backup and restore.
  • A SOC 2 pack for organizations that put their install in an audit: a control map, vendor duties, questionnaire answers and sample policies, in docs/soc2.

On your phone

SignuDoc works on small screens as well as large ones: check on your documents from your phone, and signers sign from theirs.

SignuDoc and DocuSign, side by side

DocuSign does more, and charges for it per user. SignuDoc does the everyday signing loop well, and it's yours. DocuSign's plans are as DocuSign listed them in November 2026, for the US.

Price and ownership

SignuDoc DocuSign eSignature
Price Free and open source, on free plans from Vercel, Neon and Resend $11 (Personal), $30 (Standard) or $45 (Business Pro) per user a month, on an annual plan
Envelopes No limit of its own. The free plans carry about 250 a month 5 a month on Personal, 100 per user a year on Standard and Business Pro
Where it runs Your Vercel account, with your Neon database and Blob store DocuSign's cloud
Where data is kept The region you choose, the EU included DocuSign's data centers, the EU included
Source code MIT license, on GitHub Closed
Your own domain and branding ✅ your domain, logo and color, in every install Logo and colors from Standard

The signing loop

SignuDoc DocuSign eSignature
Signing without an account ✅ ✅
Signing order ✅ in order, at the same time, or mixed, up to 25 signers ✅ in order, at the same time, or mixed
People who only get a copy ✅ ✅ and more roles: approvers, editors, in-person signers
Field types ✅ signature, initials, date, name, text, number, checkbox, dropdown, radio, each required or optional ✅ more types; dropdown, radio and signer attachments need Business Pro
Templates ✅ ✅ from Personal, shared from Standard
Send one template to many from a CSV ✅ one envelope per row, up to 200 a batch ✅ bulk send on Business Pro
Deadlines and automatic reminders ✅ ✅
Access code and emailed one-time code ✅ ✅ plus SMS, phone, knowledge-based questions and ID checks, as paid add-ons
Consent to electronic records ✅ versioned, recorded in the audit trail ✅
Sealed PDF and certificate of completion ✅ PAdES seal, self-signed by default or your own trusted certificate, long-term validation (B-LTA) with a timestamp server ✅ seal trusted by PDF readers
Audit trail ✅ hash-chained, and sent to your SIEM through a log drain ✅
Checking a signed copy ✅ the seal in a PDF reader, and a public Verify page on your own site ✅ the seal in a PDF reader
Retention rules and signer data requests ✅ built in ✅
Phones ✅ in the browser ✅ native iPhone and Android apps
Two-step sign-in ✅ authenticator app, and administrators can require it ✅
Single sign-on ✅ OpenID Connect, in every install ✅ SAML, on Enhanced, priced by sales
API and webhooks ✅ an API with keys, signed webhooks, and signing inside your own site, in every install ✅ API plans from $50 a month

Where DocuSign does more

SignuDoc DocuSign eSignature
More than one document per envelope, and Word files — PDF only, one per envelope ✅
Web forms, payments — ✅ on Business Pro
Integrations — none built in; connect your own apps through the API and webhooks ✅ 1,000+, including Salesforce, Microsoft and Google
Languages — signing pages in English ✅ signing in 44 languages
Advanced and qualified signatures (eIDAS) With a provider you add: eID Easy or a CSC remote signing service ✅
HIPAA, 21 CFR Part 11, certifications Part 11 mode and a SOC 2 pack; you validate and get audited ✅ on Enhanced or as add-ons
Support GitHub issues ✅ 24/7 on Enhanced

If your agreements run through Salesforce, need SMS checks or ID document checks, or go out by the thousand in bulk, DocuSign earns its price. If you want to send everyday agreements, keep the evidence, and own the whole thing, SignuDoc is built for you.

What it costs

SignuDoc is free, and the Deploy button puts it on free plans from Vercel, Neon and Resend. Those plans carry about 250 documents a month, however many people send them, before anything costs money. That is the first row below, and the rows after it are what you pay once you pass it.

Documents sent in a year SignuDoc DocuSign Standard DocuSign Business Pro
3,000: 250 a month, the most the free plans carry $0 $10,800, for 30 seats $16,200, for 30 seats
5,000: the most DocuSign's listed plans include $240, for Vercel Pro $18,000, for 50 seats $27,000, for 50 seats
7,200: 600 a month, the most Resend's free plan will email $240 Quoted by sales Quoted by sales
More than that $480, for Vercel Pro and Resend Pro, plus use Quoted by sales Quoted by sales

DocuSign includes 100 envelopes per user a year, so its price for a number of documents is the seats it takes to send them. SignuDoc has no seats. A team of 15, for example:

Where the $0 limit comes from

Each free plan has its own monthly allowance, and the smallest one sets the limit:

The free plan allows Which carries
Files, on Vercel Blob 2,000 uploads, 10,000 reads and 1 GB stored About 250 documents a month. A two-signer document takes 7 to 9 uploads, from the first PDF to the sealed copy and its certificates, and about 20 reads. 1 GB keeps over 1,000 finished documents of a few pages each.
Email, on Resend 3,000 emails, and no more than 100 a day 600 two-signer documents a month, and 20 in one day. Each takes five emails: two invitations and three finished copies. Reminders and one-time codes are emails too.
Database, on Neon 1 GB and 100 compute hours About 400 hours a month with the database awake. It sleeps when nobody is using the site.
Hosting, on Vercel Hobby More than the rows above will use Any number of people. Vercel limits Hobby to personal, non-commercial use.

Daily backups are off unless you turn them on. On Vercel Hobby a backup store in the same account shares the same free Blob storage. It holds about as much as the install's own files, plus copies of the database, so turning backups on leaves room for fewer than half as many finished documents.

None of these plans bills you for going over. It stops instead: files cannot be read, email is not sent, or the database pauses. The monthly allowances come back when the month turns over. The two 1 GB limits do not, because stored files and database rows stay until they are deleted: make room by deleting old documents, or by setting how long finished documents are kept under Settings, Organization. Better still, move up before you reach a limit, not after.

Past the free plans

  • Vercel Pro is $20 a month for the one person who deploys, whatever the size of the team. The people who send and sign need no Vercel seat. It lifts the file limits: Blob is then paid from the plan's $20 monthly credit, at $0.023 per GB a month. A company belongs on Pro from the start, because of Vercel's rule for Hobby.
  • Resend Pro is $20 a month for 50,000 emails, with no daily limit.
  • Neon's Launch plan charges for what the database uses, with no monthly minimum.
  • Your own domain, if you want one, costs whatever your registrar charges. Vercel Pro includes one free for the first year.

DocuSign's figures are its US list prices for annual plans in November 2026: $30 a user a month on Standard and $45 on Business Pro. Those plans stop at 50 users, and larger ones are quoted. The document counts are estimates for two signers and PDFs of a few pages; more signers, longer documents and reminders use more. Prices and free plans change, so check them before you quote these.

Get started

Deploy to Vercel

  1. Click Deploy to Vercel above, and sign in to Vercel. It copies SignuDoc into your GitHub account and builds your site from that copy.
  2. Add the three things Vercel offers to create, each on a free plan: Resend for email, a Neon Postgres database, and a private Vercel Blob store.
  3. Click Deploy. The build creates the database tables by itself. If Vercel stops with "One or more integration resources failed to provision", nothing is wrong with your copy: Resend was still checking its domain. Wait a minute or two, refresh the page, and click Redeploy. See If the first deployment fails.
  4. Open your new site. Name your organization, give the email address people should write to for help, and create the first account, which is the administrator.
  5. Set up the address you send from. Under Settings, Organization, enter an address at your own domain. The site lists the DNS records to add and checks them for you.

Taking new versions. Settings, SignuDoc, Check for updates tells you when a new release is out and what is in it. A workflow that comes with your copy then opens a pull request with the release in your GitHub repository; merge it and Vercel deploys the update. See Keep your install up to date.

Deploying with an AI agent. An agent that can use your browser can do all of this for you. Point it at docs/deploy-with-an-agent.md, which lists every screen, what to choose, what to ask you, and how to retry.

There is nothing to type in Vercel and no terminal to open. Until step 5 is done, email reaches only the address on your Resend account, so you can try the whole product straight away by sending a document to yourself. The self-hosting guide covers your own domain, locking down a new install, keeping it up to date, running in the EU, and every optional setting.

Try it on your computer

With Node.js 24 and Docker:

npm install
cp .env.example .env
npm run db:start   # Postgres in Docker, with the schema applied
npm run dev        # SignuDoc at http://localhost:3000

Files stay on disk and emails are written to .data/outbox instead of being sent, so you need no outside account. Development says more.

Built on Vercel

  • Vercel-native from end to end. Next.js 16 on Vercel Functions, Neon Postgres and Resend from the Vercel Marketplace, private Vercel Blob storage with direct browser uploads, daily Vercel cron jobs for reminders, cleanup, backups and webhook retries, and optional Vercel BotID.
  • Secure by default. Private file storage with no public URLs, a strict Content Security Policy, rate limits kept in Postgres, signing links that are hashed at rest, sign-in lockout, and a setup page that only the first visitor, or the holder of a SETUP_TOKEN, can use.
  • Tested. Unit tests, database tests against a real Postgres, and a browser test that sets up a fresh install, sends a document and signs it, run on every pull request.

Using SignuDoc for real agreements

SignuDoc is not a law firm and does not give legal advice, and nothing here is a promise that a signature made with it will be accepted for a given purpose. It gives you the features that electronic signature laws such as the US ESIGN Act and UETA and the EU's eIDAS regulation look for in a simple electronic signature: each signer's consent to electronic records, a record of who signed, when and how, optional identity checks, and a sealed copy that shows any change. Whether that is enough for a particular document depends on the document, where you and the signers are, and how you use it. Ask a lawyer when it matters.

Every install has a page at /electronic-signatures that says what it is for, and senders confirm it before each send. It is meant for ordinary business agreements, such as contracts, NDAs, statements of work, offer letters, purchase orders and approvals. It is not built for:

  • documents that need an advanced or qualified electronic signature (AdES or QES) under eIDAS, unless you add a signing provider (see below);
  • protected health information under HIPAA;
  • documents that many laws keep out of electronic signature, such as wills, family-law matters, court orders, notices of foreclosure, eviction, utility shut-off or insurance cancellation, and in most EU countries real estate transfers and documents that need a notary.

For advanced or qualified electronic signatures under eIDAS, connect a signing provider: eID Easy, or a trust service provider's remote signing service that speaks the CSC API v2. A sender can then choose that signature type for an envelope, and each signer proves who they are at the provider and signs with a certificate in their own name. Every signature goes into the PDF in a revision of its own, so all of them stay valid, and the finished PDF gets long-term validation. The provider is a paid service outside Vercel, so it is optional, and the flow has been tested against stand-ins for both interfaces but not yet against the live services. Signatures in the signers' own names has the setup.

For FDA 21 CFR Part 11 records, an administrator can turn on Part 11 mode under Settings. Signers then sign with their own accounts, whose identity an administrator has confirmed, give their password again at each signature, and see the meaning of their signature (approval, review, responsibility or authorship) printed beside it with their name and the time. Audit trails export as CSV, and finished records are never deleted on a timer. That covers the software's part only: validating your install, writing and following your own procedures, training your people and certifying your electronic signatures to the FDA stay with your organization. The Part 11 validation pack gives you starting documents for that: requirements, a traceability matrix, a risk assessment, qualification scripts, SOP templates and the FDA letter.

Your install carries your organization's name, and your organization is responsible for how it is used: linking your own terms and privacy policy, keeping the support address pointed at a mailbox someone reads, choosing how long documents are kept, and answering signers' data requests. Your responsibilities has the details.

⭐️⭐️⭐️ Open-source, self-hosted alternative to Linear and Plane. Project management and issue tracking where teams and AI agents work side by side to plan and ship products.

https://itsaplan.dev/

The open-source Linear alternative
where AI agents take issues like teammates

Use it as a regular issue tracker from day one. When you are ready, give an agent an issue the way you give it to a colleague, and review the result yourself or let another agent check it. Put agents on a schedule, or build a workflow that passes an issue from agent to agent. Self-hosted, on your own server.

If It's a Plan looks useful to you, star the repo ⭐ and leave a review on Product Hunt.
For news and updates, follow us on Threads.

Trusted by

All teams · Add your team →

Why It's a Plan

  • Agents as project members. Each gets a role, permissions and an assignee slot, and works on the same board as your people.
  • Two kinds of agents. Internal agents run on your server, on any model with your API key. External agents run on your machine through @itsaplan/runner, under your own Claude Code, Codex, Copilot CLI or opencode account.
  • Any kind of work. Software, marketing, design, support, sales, operations, research.
  • Yours to run. Your server and your database.

Community features

Area What you get
Product management Kanban, table, timeline, and calendar views · cycles · custom fields · dashboards · docs · notes boards · project templates · import from Linear, Trello, and Plane
AI agents Agents as project members · internal on any model, or external on your coding CLI · runs start on an @mention, an assignment, or a schedule
Platform REST API with OpenAPI · MCP server · webhooks · pull requests from 5 forges · SSO over OIDC and SCIM · passkeys and Google sign-in
14 languages English · Українська · Русский · 简体中文 · 繁體中文 · العربية · Français · فارسی · Português (Brasil) · Bahasa Indonesia · Español · 한국어 · Türkçe · Italiano
Product management: the full list
  • Configure issues per project: custom fields, labels, states, and issue types
  • Kanban, table, timeline, and calendar views. Save a view as a tab with its own filters, fields, and two-level grouping, for the whole project or only for you. Each person orders and hides their own tabs
  • Cycles that time-box the work. Unfinished issues move to the next cycle
  • Subtasks, checklists, attachments, and links between issues: blocks, relates, duplicates
  • Comment threads with replies, and @mentions of people and agents
  • Project dashboards: throughput, burnup with a projected completion date, breakdown, and pulse
  • Quick actions on an issue, and automatic assignment when an issue moves to a state
  • Docs: Markdown pages in a tree, with revision history, private and locked pages, embedded files, comments, @mentions, and links to issues
  • Notes boards: sticky notes on a canvas, with colors, checklists, and connections
  • Share a view, an issue, or a document by public link, read-only and without sign-in
  • Initiatives that group and track related work inside a project
  • Project templates: save a project as a template for your team, or publish it to the gallery at itsaplan.dev
  • Import projects from Linear, Trello, and Plane
  • Auto-archive, a notification inbox, and role-based access control
AI agents: the full list
  • Agents as project members, with their own permissions and assigned issues
  • Internal agents run on the instance. Configure the model, system prompt, tools, and reusable skills, written inline or imported from a GitHub repository
  • External agents run on your machine, under your own account. @itsaplan/runner gives each task to Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity CLI, GitHub Copilot CLI, opencode, Pi, Oh My Pi, Mastra Code, or any command that reads stdin
  • Your own code can also take tasks from the run queue through the API
  • A run starts on an @mention in a comment on an issue or a document, on an assignment, or on a schedule. A schedule starts on a timer or when an issue moves to a state
  • Tokens and cost of every run, by agent, project, and model
  • Tools for other services: Notion, Baserow, Telegram, Slack, Threads, Instagram, Jina, Firecrawl, Keenable, DataForSEO, Gitea, Forgejo, GitHub, and GitLab
  • Images, video, music, and speech from the models on Kie: Nano Banana, Seedream, Kling, Veo, Suno, and others, with one API key
  • Chat with each agent, with its own history. Turn chat off for an agent that only works on mentions, assignments, and schedules
  • Chat with an external agent too. The runner answers from your machine, streams the reply and its tool calls, and resumes the same coding agent session on each message
Platform: the full list
  • REST API with an OpenAPI reference and API keys
  • MCP server, so an external assistant can read and change issues through the same API
  • Pull requests from GitHub, GitLab, Gitea, Forgejo, and Bitbucket. "Fixes KEY-42" links the pull request to the issue, and the issue moves when the pull request opens and merges
  • Outgoing webhooks for the events you pick, with signed payloads, retries, and a delivery log
  • Sign-in with an email or username and a password, a passkey, Google, or your identity provider over OIDC. SCIM keeps accounts in sync with your directory
  • Notifications by email (SMTP, Resend, or Microsoft 365), Telegram, and Slack, with preferences for each member
  • Instance administration: storage limits, the mail provider, and instance-wide settings

Pro edition

Bring the whole team. Pro adds full control over workspaces, agents and spend.

Tip

$240 a year for the whole instance, 1 person or 500. Fast Deploy installs Pro on your own server in about 5 minutes.

Everything in Community, plus:

  • Fast Deploy
  • Unlimited workspaces
  • SAML or OIDC per workspace
  • SCIM per workspace
  • Workspace dashboard
  • Audit log
  • Agent workflows
  • Schedules on issue events
  • Agent cost by person, trigger and workflow
  • AI budgets
  • Public forms

See what each feature does →

Three ways to run Pro:

  • Fast Deploy installs Pro on your own Hetzner, Vultr or DigitalOcean server in about 5 minutes. Updates take one click.
  • Railway: the template runs Pro in one click.
  • By hand: deploy on Docker, Coolify or Kubernetes.

On Railway and by hand, enter the key in god mode under License. Without a valid key, Pro runs as Community. Your data stays when you switch editions.

Getting started

Deploy on Railway — recommended

The whole stack in one click, with no server to maintain. You give Railway two hostnames, and it generates every secret. You need a domain of your own: the guide explains why, and what to do after the deploy.

Fast Deploy for Pro

With a Pro license, Fast Deploy installs Pro on a new server in your Hetzner, Vultr or DigitalOcean account. See Pro edition.

Try it on your machine

Requirements: Docker and Bun.

git clone https://github.com/croffasia/itsaplan.git
cd itsaplan
bun install
bun run setup   # answer "Try it"

It picks free ports, generates the secrets, starts the whole stack in Docker, and opens http://localhost:3001. Everything runs on localhost, so no domain and no reverse proxy are needed. Run it again later to restart the instance; the data stays.

Everything else

  • Deploy on Railway — one-click hosted deploy from the template
  • Self-hosting — the full production setup, secrets, and updates
  • Deploy on Coolify — the same stack on a Coolify instance
  • Deploy on Kubernetes — Helm chart for any Kubernetes cluster
  • Local development — running the apps on the host, and the tests
  • Coding agent setup — the config for each CLI that @itsaplan/runner runs
  • Agent endpoint — the instance sends an external agent's tasks to a URL that you run, such as an AWS Lambda function

Built with

Layer Technology
Runtime Bun + Turborepo
Backend Elysia
Frontend Next.js App Router, SSR
UI shadcn/ui + Tailwind v4
Auth better-auth
Database Drizzle + PostgreSQL
Storage S3-compatible object store (RustFS)
AI agents Mastra

Contributing

Issues and pull requests are welcome — bug fixes, features, docs, all of it. Start with CONTRIBUTING.md. It covers the setup, the conventions, and how a change gets merged. Be kind; we follow a Code of Conduct.

Thank you to everyone who has contributed to It's a Plan:

Not ready to contribute code? Star the repo and share it — it is the simplest way to help the project grow.

Security

Found a vulnerability? Report it privately through GitHub Security Advisories, not a public issue, so we can fix it first. Details in SECURITY.md.

AGPL-3.0, except packages/runner, which is Apache-2.0.
